### 3.2. Generating stationary-phase promoters using DiPro
To design novel promoters with desired functions, we employed a masking strategy by providing a partially masked sequence for the model to generate the missing area. First, stationary-phase promoters were collected and analyzed according to their strength. Stationary-phase promoters regulated by σ38, also known as RpoS [ 32 ], exhibit pronounced AT-rich extended −10 features [ 33 ], weaker −35 dependence, and −35/−10 spacing concentrated at 16–18 bp, with distinctive composition between −10 and the TSS. σ38-annotated samples were included during training, and stationary-phase–targeted sequences were generated by inpainting: for each high-expression σ38 seed, multiple non-overlapping 6-mer windows were masked and completed by the diffusion model, preserving global spacing while reshaping local content. This strategy yielded 5000 candidates. Each candidate was encoded as an 87-dimensional feature vector and the dimensionality was reduced to 10 via PCA. Bayesian clustering using a full-covariance GMM was then applied in this reduced space. The number of clusters was objectively determined by scanning K from 2 to 10 and selecting the value that minimized the BIC, which identified K = 3 as the optimal model ( Fig. S3 ). The resulting GMM partitioned the candidates into three compositionally distinct groups with calibrated posterior probabilities ( Fig. 3 A).
Conditional generation and clustering of stationary-phase (σ 38 -regulated) promoters.

### 3.3. Characterizing the activity of generated stationary phase promoters
The transcriptional activity of the generated stationary-phase promoters was evaluated using GFP as a reporter [ 34 ]. Fluorescence intensity was monitored at key time points (10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 45, 50, 55 and 60 h, consistent with Fig. 5 ) throughout a 60 h fermentation period to fully capture the temporal transcriptional activity and stationary-phase-specific activation pattern ( Fig. 4 ). To ensure representativeness and structural diversity for reliable experimental validation, 60 promoter candidates were strictly selected from 5000 generated sequences based on four quantitative criteria: (1) balanced sampling across clusters with 20 candidates selected from each of Cluster 0, Cluster 1, and Cluster 2; (2) high-confidence filtering with a GMM posterior classification probability of no less than 0.7; (3) preference for candidates harboring conserved −35/−10 core motifs and canonical 16–18 bp spacer length; (4) removal of sequences with over 90% identity to eliminate redundant sequences and maximize structural diversity. Promoter sequences were randomly selected from each computationally defined cluster for experimental validation ( Table S1 ). To more specifically and rigorously evaluate the stationary-phase activity of synthetic promoters, two well-characterized σ 38 -regulated native stationary-phase promoters, P katE and P bola , were included as stationary-phase positive controls, in addition to the strong constitutive promoter J23119 (as a general strength benchmark). Our results demonstrated that 49 out of the 60 tested promoters (81.6%) exhibited significantly higher activity than the negative control. However, all synthetic promoters showed lower strength than the strong constitutive promoter J23119 ( Fig. 4 ), which is one of the most active constitutive promoters [ 35 ] and was used as a general positive control for promoter strength. Among the generated promoters, the most active one, P11, reached 79.6% of the total activity of J23119, and more import

### 3.4. Characterizing time-dependent activity of the generated stationary-phase promoters
Next, we characterized the time-dependent activity of the generated promoters by tracking the OD 600 and fluorescent intensity of the top 20 most active designs. To eliminate ambiguity and enable quantitative classification, we strictly defined four growth phases based on fermentation time: (1) Exponential growth phase: 0–20 h (rapid OD 600 increase, negligible stationary-phase promoter activity); (2) Early stationary phase: 20–30 h (OD 600 stabilization, initial promoter activation); (3) Middle stationary phase: 30–50 h (peak promoter activity); (4) Late stationary phase: 50–60 h (sustained activity under nutrient limitation). Promoters were categorized by the first time point of significant fluorescence elevation relative to the exponential phase. The time-dependent activation profiles of the native stationary-phase promoters P katE and P bola were also monitored as references, and both exhibited typical mid-stationary-phase activation characteristics, which were consistent with the main activation trend of our synthetic promoters. We found that 14 promoters were active before the 20 h time point, when OD 600 stabilized, indicating they are not strictly stationary-phase promoters ( Fig. 5 ). Furthermore, even among stationary-phase promoters, we observed variation in their timing of activation, likely due to sensing different cellular stresses. Based on the above quantitative time criteria, we divided the stationary phase into three periods: early, middle, and late. We found that 20% and 60% of these promoters were activated in the early and middle phases, respectively, and displayed higher overall induction activity than those activated late. This may be attributed to the relatively abundant nutrient availability during the early to middle stationary phase, whereas promoters induced later are likely constrained by nutrient depletion and deteriorating environmental conditions.

### 3.5. Induction of cell lysis using stationary phase promoters, a case study
As a proof-of-concept for the functional application of our designed promoters, we implemented a programmed cell lysis system using stationary-phase-specific promoters to control the expression of a lethal protein. To rigorously validate lysis efficiency, the negative control without the CoIM cassette and the strong constitutive promoter J23119 (added in Fig. 6 B) were included as controls. We selected three of the strongest generated promoters, each demonstrating activation during the early (P05), middle (P14), and late (P11) stationary phase, respectively. These promoters were used to drive the expression of the cell lysis protein CoIM ( Fig. 6 A), which was chosen for its previously reported high efficacy in degrading E. coli cell walls even under high-density cultivation conditions [ 36 ]. The performance of this system was evaluated by monitoring the growth of engineered strains over a 60 h fermentation period. As shown in Fig. 6 B, the negative control strain, which lacked the CoIM expression cassette, exhibited robust growth, reaching a final OD 600 of approximately 8. The constitutive promoter J23119 mediated complete cell lysis and served as the positive control for maximal lysis activity. In stark contrast, strains carrying the CoIM gene under the control of the synthetic promoters showed markedly impaired growth, confirming the functional triggering of cell lysis.
Schematic of the cell lysis experiment.

### 4. Discussion
This study developed a stable diffusion-based model, DiPro, for the de novo generation of promoters. Initial analyses demonstrated that the designed promoters accurately recapitulated key features of the natural training set, as evidenced by sequence logos, k-mer spectra, and functional motif distributions [ 37 ]. We then employed DiPro to design stationary-phase promoters by inpainting randomly masked regions within seed sequences. Subsequently, we developed a Bayesian-based machine learning model to cluster the generated promoters. Representative samples from each cluster were experimentally characterized, revealing that 81.6% exhibited induction activity. Furthermore, we found that these stationary-phase promoters were activated during three distinct stages (early, middle, and late). Leveraging this temporal precision, we used selected promoters to drive expression of the cell lysis protein CoIM, thereby regulating cell death. Notably, promoter P05 triggered cell lysis with high efficiency. This work establishes a novel methodological framework and validates its practical utility.
Generative networks are now well-established for promoter design. Pioneering GAN-based models demonstrated the feasibility of designing functional E. coli promoters [ 15 ], and when combined with a predictive network, enabled the design of promoters with tunable activity levels. Subsequently, GAN-based frameworks were adapted for designing eukaryotic promoters [ 16 ], enabling applications in Saccharomyces cerevisiae with potential extension to filamentous fungi and microalgae [ 38 ]. In more recent work, diffusion models have been applied. However, early implementations relied on a separate promoter recognition model to guide generation [ 39 ]. This limitation has been addressed by later approaches. Unconditional de novo generation and functional validation of synthetic promoters with a diffusion model

### Abstract
Generative neural networks enable de novo design of synthetic genetic elements. Here, we present DiPro, an unconditional diffusion model that learns E. coli promoter features to generate novel sequences without conditional input. DiPro directly generates 50-bp promoter sequences from Gaussian noise using a time-conditioned Transformer denoiser, without auxiliary discriminators or recognizers. DiPro accurately recapitulates natural promoter statistics, including sequence motifs, k-mer spectra, conserved −35/−10 spacing (16–18 bp). Over 90% of generated sequences were classified as real promoters by an independent recognizer, indicating high structural fidelity. To design stationary-phase–specific promoters, generation was guided by inpainting randomly masked regions (three non-overlapping 6-mers, 18 bp) within sigma38-associated (σ 38 ) seed sequences, yielding 5000 candidates while preserving global promoter architecture. Bayesian classification resolved these sequences into three distinct clusters with divergent −35/−10 composition and motif conservation. Experimentally, 81.6% of tested promoters exhibited stationary-phase activity, with the strongest variant reaching 79.6% of the activity of the constitutive promoter J23119. Promoters displayed distinct activation timing, reflecting heterogeneous stress responses. As a proof-of-concept, selected promoters were used to drive a lysis protein, achieving phase-specific and tunable cell lysis that matched promoter activation timing, with early-phase promoters reducing culture density to an optical density at 600 nm of approximately 1.5–2.0. Together, these results establish DiPro as a generative framework for creating functional bacterial promoters with programmable temporal dynamics, offering a new tool for synthetic biology and metabolic engineering.

### 1. Introduction
Promoters are essential cis -regulatory DNA sequences that control the transcription rate of downstream genes and thereby determine protein expression levels in living cells [ 1 ]. The activity of promoters directly influences both protein abundance and secretion efficiency, making them critical targets for optimizing recombinant protein production and metabolic flux in microorganisms [ 2 , 3 ]. Despite extensive efforts to engineer strong constitutive promoters, it remains challenging to design promoters with activities surpassing those of the strongest natural counterparts or time-dependent samples that regulates cell behavior at specific period [ 4 , 5 ]. In Escherichia coli , growth-phase–dependent promoters exhibit dynamic transcriptional activity that varies across exponential and stationary phases, enabling precise temporal regulation of gene expression [ 6 , 7 ]. These promoters are controlled by cellular physiological states and global regulators such as σ 70 , ensuring coordinated responses to environmental and metabolic changes [ 8 ]. Understanding and engineering such phase-specific promoters is crucial for optimizing dynamic gene expression in synthetic and metabolic circuits [ 9 ]. Their rational design can improve time-dependent protein production, stress adaptation, and lifespan control in engineered microbial systems [ 10 ].
Bioinformatics tools have long been used to dissect promoter sequence–function relationships and to guide de novo design by identifying conserved features such as the −35 and −10 motifs and their optimal spacing [ 11 ]. These motif-centric and statistical approaches together with synthetic-library screens have clarified key determinants of promoter strength, for example, the TTTACG/−35 and TATAAT/−10 combination and an ∼17-bp spacer [ 12 ], but they struggle to capture the higher-order, nonlinear interactions among sequence elements that ultimately govern activity, leaving accurate strength prediction challenging [ 13 ]. ### 2.5. Model architecture
DiPro is a diffusion language model (DLM) built on a Transformer [ 28 ] backbone comprising an embedding layer, a time-conditioned encoder, and a diffusion module, as shown in Fig. 1 . Tokens are embedded in a 512-dimensional space and normalized with LayerNorm. The encoder stacks 12 layers with 8-head self-attention and GELU feed-forward blocks at fourfold width, using rotary position embeddings (RoPE) for positional encoding. Diffusion time is injected via adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN): a learned sinusoidal time embedding produces per-layer scale (γ) and shift (β) that modulate normalized activations:
Schematic of the DiPro model architecture and workflow.
The model takes Gaussian noise (z ∼ N(0,I)) and time step (t) as inputs, with token embedding (10 tokens, 512 dimensions) and learned sinusoidal time embedding (128 dimensions) fed into a time-conditioned Transformer denoiser. The denoiser comprises multi-head attention (8 heads, RoPE-32), AdaLayerNorm (AdaLN), and feed-forward networks (FFN, 512→2048→512); reverse diffusion iteratively refines the noisy input to generate 50-bp promoter sequences. Training losses include diffusion loss (MSE) and reconstruction loss (CE); the output projection layer and LM Head produce logits, with ArgMax used to decode final DNA sequences. ### 2.6. Diffusion process
We use a continuous-time diffusion framework [ 29 ] with t ∈ [0, 1] . In training, forward diffusion adds Gaussian noise to the clean embedding X 0 :
X t = √(γ(t)) X 0 + √(1-γ(t)) ε, ε ∼ N(0, I),
cos 2 (( (t + 0.0002))/(2 (1.00025))) . Time steps t are sampled uniformly from U(0.001, 0.999) to avoid degenerate extremes. During inference, reverse diffusion starts from pure Gaussian noise z and iteratively denoises with the trained Transformer estimator, updating at each step as
X t -Δ t = √(γ(t-Δ t)) f θ (X t , t) + √(1-γ(t-Δ t)) ε'.

### 2.8. Evaluation of generated sequence quality
We conducted a multi-level quantitative comparison between generated promoters and the training set to assess sequence quality and functional fidelity. First, we used information-theoretic sequence logos derived from per-position base frequencies and Shannon entropy, with I = 2 - H and H = -∑ p i
p i , to visualize conservation at key regulatory elements such as the −35 and −10 boxes. This approach quantifies positional specificity and provides direct evidence for the preservation of core regulatory motifs.

### 3.1. Establishing DiPro to unconditional generate de novo promoters
We introduce DiPro, an unconditional diffusion framework for de novo generation of non-natural promoters. The model starts from Gaussian noise and, through a time-conditioned Transformer denoiser, iteratively generates 50-bp promoter sequences without relying on an auxiliary discriminator or a separate recognizer ( Fig. 1 ). DiPro was benchmarked against three representative deep generative models for promoter design, including generative adversarial networks, variational autoencoders, and early diffusion-based generative tools. The performance was assessed by comparing conserved motifs, spatial distributions of key motifs, and the −35 to −10 spacing statistics ( Fig. 2 A). To select the training epochs with the best performance, we visualized the sequence-logo comparisons of sequences generated during training and predicted the real promoter portion (RPP, defined as the fraction of generated sequences classified as authentic promoters by PromoR) in the generated data using PromoR [ 31 ], a tool previously shown to achieve high accuracy in classifying real and artificial promoters ( Fig. 1 C and D).
Unconditional de novo generation of Escherichia coli promoters by DiPro recapitulates natural promoter features.
(A) Sequence logos of natural promoters and DiPro-generated promoters (post-training) aligned to the transcription start site (TSS). Both sets exhibit conserved −35 and −10 regions, with the classical TT motif at −35 and TATAAT motif at −10 showing consistent positional alignment. (B) Real Promoter Portion (RPP) of generated sequences (assessed by PromoR) across training epochs, reaching &gt;90% stability after 600 epochs. (C) K-mer spectrum correlation between natural and DiPro-generated promoters. 2-mer to 6-mer distributions show high agreement, with a Pearson correlation coefficient (r) of 0.997 for 2-mers; point-wise regression at 6-mer resolution yields R 2 = 0.859, highlighting accurate recapitulation of key motifs (e.g., TATAAT). ### 3.2. Generating stationary-phase promoters using DiPro
To design novel promoters with desired functions, we employed a masking strategy by providing a partially masked sequence for the model to generate the missing area. First, stationary-phase promoters were collected and analyzed according to their strength. Stationary-phase promoters regulated by σ38, also known as RpoS [ 32 ], exhibit pronounced AT-rich extended −10 features [ 33 ], weaker −35 dependence, and −35/−10 spacing concentrated at 16–18 bp, with distinctive composition between −10 and the TSS. σ38-annotated samples were included during training, and stationary-phase–targeted sequences were generated by inpainting: for each high-expression σ38 seed, multiple non-overlapping 6-mer windows were masked and completed by the diffusion model, preserving global spacing while reshaping local content. This strategy yielded 5000 candidates. Each candidate was encoded as an 87-dimensional feature vector and the dimensionality was reduced to 10 via PCA. Bayesian clustering using a full-covariance GMM was then applied in this reduced space. The number of clusters was objectively determined by scanning K from 2 to 10 and selecting the value that minimized the BIC, which identified K = 3 as the optimal model ( Fig. S3 ). The resulting GMM partitioned the candidates into three compositionally distinct groups with calibrated posterior probabilities ( Fig. 3 A).
Conditional generation and clustering of stationary-phase (σ 38 -regulated) promoters.

### 3.3. Characterizing the activity of generated stationary phase promoters
The transcriptional activity of the generated stationary-phase promoters was evaluated using GFP as a reporter [ 34 ]. Fluorescence intensity was monitored at key time points (10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 45, 50, 55 and 60 h, consistent with Fig. 5 ) throughout a 60 h fermentation period to fully capture the temporal transcriptional activity and stationary-phase-specific activation pattern ( Fig. 4 ). To ensure representativeness and structural diversity for reliable experimental validation, 60 promoter candidates were strictly selected from 5000 generated sequences based on four quantitative criteria: (1) balanced sampling across clusters with 20 candidates selected from each of Cluster 0, Cluster 1, and Cluster 2; (2) high-confidence filtering with a GMM posterior classification probability of no less than 0.7; (3) preference for candidates harboring conserved −35/−10 core motifs and canonical 16–18 bp spacer length; (4) removal of sequences with over 90% identity to eliminate redundant sequences and maximize structural diversity. Promoter sequences were randomly selected from each computationally defined cluster for experimental validation ( Table S1 ). To more specifically and rigorously evaluate the stationary-phase activity of synthetic promoters, two well-characterized σ 38 -regulated native stationary-phase promoters, P katE and P bola , were included as stationary-phase positive controls, in addition to the strong constitutive promoter J23119 (as a general strength benchmark). Our results demonstrated that 49 out of the 60 tested promoters (81.6%) exhibited significantly higher activity than the negative control. However, all synthetic promoters showed lower strength than the strong constitutive promoter J23119 ( Fig. 4 ), which is one of the most active constitutive promoters [ 35 ] and was used as a general positive control for promoter strength. Among the generated promoters, the most active one, P11, reached 79.6% of the total activity of J23119, and more import

### 3.4. Characterizing time-dependent activity of the generated stationary-phase promoters
Next, we characterized the time-dependent activity of the generated promoters by tracking the OD 600 and fluorescent intensity of the top 20 most active designs. To eliminate ambiguity and enable quantitative classification, we strictly defined four growth phases based on fermentation time: (1) Exponential growth phase: 0–20 h (rapid OD 600 increase, negligible stationary-phase promoter activity); (2) Early stationary phase: 20–30 h (OD 600 stabilization, initial promoter activation); (3) Middle stationary phase: 30–50 h (peak promoter activity); (4) Late stationary phase: 50–60 h (sustained activity under nutrient limitation). Promoters were categorized by the first time point of significant fluorescence elevation relative to the exponential phase. The time-dependent activation profiles of the native stationary-phase promoters P katE and P bola were also monitored as references, and both exhibited typical mid-stationary-phase activation characteristics, which were consistent with the main activation trend of our synthetic promoters. We found that 14 promoters were active before the 20 h time point, when OD 600 stabilized, indicating they are not strictly stationary-phase promoters ( Fig. 5 ). Furthermore, even among stationary-phase promoters, we observed variation in their timing of activation, likely due to sensing different cellular stresses. Based on the above quantitative time criteria, we divided the stationary phase into three periods: early, middle, and late. We found that 20% and 60% of these promoters were activated in the early and middle phases, respectively, and displayed higher overall induction activity than those activated late. This may be attributed to the relatively abundant nutrient availability during the early to middle stationary phase, whereas promoters induced later are likely constrained by nutrient depletion and deteriorating environmental conditions.

### 3.5. Induction of cell lysis using stationary phase promoters, a case study
As a proof-of-concept for the functional application of our designed promoters, we implemented a programmed cell lysis system using stationary-phase-specific promoters to control the expression of a lethal protein. To rigorously validate lysis efficiency, the negative control without the CoIM cassette and the strong constitutive promoter J23119 (added in Fig. 6 B) were included as controls. We selected three of the strongest generated promoters, each demonstrating activation during the early (P05), middle (P14), and late (P11) stationary phase, respectively. These promoters were used to drive the expression of the cell lysis protein CoIM ( Fig. 6 A), which was chosen for its previously reported high efficacy in degrading E. coli cell walls even under high-density cultivation conditions [ 36 ]. The performance of this system was evaluated by monitoring the growth of engineered strains over a 60 h fermentation period. As shown in Fig. 6 B, the negative control strain, which lacked the CoIM expression cassette, exhibited robust growth, reaching a final OD 600 of approximately 8. The constitutive promoter J23119 mediated complete cell lysis and served as the positive control for maximal lysis activity. In stark contrast, strains carrying the CoIM gene under the control of the synthetic promoters showed markedly impaired growth, confirming the functional triggering of cell lysis.
Schematic of the cell lysis experiment.

### 4. Discussion
This study developed a stable diffusion-based model, DiPro, for the de novo generation of promoters. Initial analyses demonstrated that the designed promoters accurately recapitulated key features of the natural training set, as evidenced by sequence logos, k-mer spectra, and functional motif distributions [ 37 ]. We then employed DiPro to design stationary-phase promoters by inpainting randomly masked regions within seed sequences. Subsequently, we developed a Bayesian-based machine learning model to cluster the generated promoters. Representative samples from each cluster were experimentally characterized, revealing that 81.6% exhibited induction activity. Furthermore, we found that these stationary-phase promoters were activated during three distinct stages (early, middle, and late). Leveraging this temporal precision, we used selected promoters to drive expression of the cell lysis protein CoIM, thereby regulating cell death. Notably, promoter P05 triggered cell lysis with high efficiency. This work establishes a novel methodological framework and validates its practical utility.
Generative networks are now well-established for promoter design. Pioneering GAN-based models demonstrated the feasibility of designing functional E. coli promoters [ 15 ], and when combined with a predictive network, enabled the design of promoters with tunable activity levels. Subsequently, GAN-based frameworks were adapted for designing eukaryotic promoters [ 16 ], enabling applications in Saccharomyces cerevisiae with potential extension to filamentous fungi and microalgae [ 38 ]. In more recent work, diffusion models have been applied. However, early implementations relied on a separate promoter recognition model to guide generation [ 39 ]. This limitation has been addressed by later approaches. Unconditional de novo generation and functional validation of synthetic promoters with a diffusion model

### Abstract
Generative neural networks enable de novo design of synthetic genetic elements. Here, we present DiPro, an unconditional diffusion model that learns E. coli promoter features to generate novel sequences without conditional input. DiPro directly generates 50-bp promoter sequences from Gaussian noise using a time-conditioned Transformer denoiser, without auxiliary discriminators or recognizers. DiPro accurately recapitulates natural promoter statistics, including sequence motifs, k-mer spectra, conserved −35/−10 spacing (16–18 bp). Over 90% of generated sequences were classified as real promoters by an independent recognizer, indicating high structural fidelity. To design stationary-phase–specific promoters, generation was guided by inpainting randomly masked regions (three non-overlapping 6-mers, 18 bp) within sigma38-associated (σ 38 ) seed sequences, yielding 5000 candidates while preserving global promoter architecture. Bayesian classification resolved these sequences into three distinct clusters with divergent −35/−10 composition and motif conservation. Experimentally, 81.6% of tested promoters exhibited stationary-phase activity, with the strongest variant reaching 79.6% of the activity of the constitutive promoter J23119. Promoters displayed distinct activation timing, reflecting heterogeneous stress responses. As a proof-of-concept, selected promoters were used to drive a lysis protein, achieving phase-specific and tunable cell lysis that matched promoter activation timing, with early-phase promoters reducing culture density to an optical density at 600 nm of approximately 1.5–2.0. Together, these results establish DiPro as a generative framework for creating functional bacterial promoters with programmable temporal dynamics, offering a new tool for synthetic biology and metabolic engineering.

### 1. Introduction
Promoters are essential cis -regulatory DNA sequences that control the transcription rate of downstream genes and thereby determine protein expression levels in living cells [ 1 ]. The activity of promoters directly influences both protein abundance and secretion efficiency, making them critical targets for optimizing recombinant protein production and metabolic flux in microorganisms [ 2 , 3 ]. Despite extensive efforts to engineer strong constitutive promoters, it remains challenging to design promoters with activities surpassing those of the strongest natural counterparts or time-dependent samples that regulates cell behavior at specific period [ 4 , 5 ]. In Escherichia coli , growth-phase–dependent promoters exhibit dynamic transcriptional activity that varies across exponential and stationary phases, enabling precise temporal regulation of gene expression [ 6 , 7 ]. These promoters are controlled by cellular physiological states and global regulators such as σ 70 , ensuring coordinated responses to environmental and metabolic changes [ 8 ]. Understanding and engineering such phase-specific promoters is crucial for optimizing dynamic gene expression in synthetic and metabolic circuits [ 9 ]. Their rational design can improve time-dependent protein production, stress adaptation, and lifespan control in engineered microbial systems [ 10 ].
Bioinformatics tools have long been used to dissect promoter sequence–function relationships and to guide de novo design by identifying conserved features such as the −35 and −10 motifs and their optimal spacing [ 11 ]. These motif-centric and statistical approaches together with synthetic-library screens have clarified key determinants of promoter strength, for example, the TTTACG/−35 and TATAAT/−10 combination and an ∼17-bp spacer [ 12 ], but they struggle to capture the higher-order, nonlinear interactions among sequence elements that ultimately govern activity, leaving accurate strength prediction challenging [ 13 ]. ### 2.5. Model architecture
DiPro is a diffusion language model (DLM) built on a Transformer [ 28 ] backbone comprising an embedding layer, a time-conditioned encoder, and a diffusion module, as shown in Fig. 1 . Tokens are embedded in a 512-dimensional space and normalized with LayerNorm. The encoder stacks 12 layers with 8-head self-attention and GELU feed-forward blocks at fourfold width, using rotary position embeddings (RoPE) for positional encoding. Diffusion time is injected via adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN): a learned sinusoidal time embedding produces per-layer scale (γ) and shift (β) that modulate normalized activations:
Schematic of the DiPro model architecture and workflow.
The model takes Gaussian noise (z ∼ N(0,I)) and time step (t) as inputs, with token embedding (10 tokens, 512 dimensions) and learned sinusoidal time embedding (128 dimensions) fed into a time-conditioned Transformer denoiser. The denoiser comprises multi-head attention (8 heads, RoPE-32), AdaLayerNorm (AdaLN), and feed-forward networks (FFN, 512→2048→512); reverse diffusion iteratively refines the noisy input to generate 50-bp promoter sequences. Training losses include diffusion loss (MSE) and reconstruction loss (CE); the output projection layer and LM Head produce logits, with ArgMax used to decode final DNA sequences. ### 2.6. Diffusion process
We use a continuous-time diffusion framework [ 29 ] with t ∈ [0, 1] . In training, forward diffusion adds Gaussian noise to the clean embedding X 0 :
X t = √(γ(t)) X 0 + √(1-γ(t)) ε, ε ∼ N(0, I),
cos 2 (( (t + 0.0002))/(2 (1.00025))) . Time steps t are sampled uniformly from U(0.001, 0.999) to avoid degenerate extremes. During inference, reverse diffusion starts from pure Gaussian noise z and iteratively denoises with the trained Transformer estimator, updating at each step as
X t -Δ t = √(γ(t-Δ t)) f θ (X t , t) + √(1-γ(t-Δ t)) ε'.

### 2.8. Evaluation of generated sequence quality
We conducted a multi-level quantitative comparison between generated promoters and the training set to assess sequence quality and functional fidelity. First, we used information-theoretic sequence logos derived from per-position base frequencies and Shannon entropy, with I = 2 - H and H = -∑ p i
p i , to visualize conservation at key regulatory elements such as the −35 and −10 boxes. This approach quantifies positional specificity and provides direct evidence for the preservation of core regulatory motifs.

### 3.1. Establishing DiPro to unconditional generate de novo promoters
We introduce DiPro, an unconditional diffusion framework for de novo generation of non-natural promoters. The model starts from Gaussian noise and, through a time-conditioned Transformer denoiser, iteratively generates 50-bp promoter sequences without relying on an auxiliary discriminator or a separate recognizer ( Fig. 1 ). DiPro was benchmarked against three representative deep generative models for promoter design, including generative adversarial networks, variational autoencoders, and early diffusion-based generative tools. The performance was assessed by comparing conserved motifs, spatial distributions of key motifs, and the −35 to −10 spacing statistics ( Fig. 2 A). To select the training epochs with the best performance, we visualized the sequence-logo comparisons of sequences generated during training and predicted the real promoter portion (RPP, defined as the fraction of generated sequences classified as authentic promoters by PromoR) in the generated data using PromoR [ 31 ], a tool previously shown to achieve high accuracy in classifying real and artificial promoters ( Fig. 1 C and D).
Unconditional de novo generation of Escherichia coli promoters by DiPro recapitulates natural promoter features.
(A) Sequence logos of natural promoters and DiPro-generated promoters (post-training) aligned to the transcription start site (TSS). Both sets exhibit conserved −35 and −10 regions, with the classical TT motif at −35 and TATAAT motif at −10 showing consistent positional alignment. (B) Real Promoter Portion (RPP) of generated sequences (assessed by PromoR) across training epochs, reaching &gt;90% stability after 600 epochs. (C) K-mer spectrum correlation between natural and DiPro-generated promoters. 2-mer to 6-mer distributions show high agreement, with a Pearson correlation coefficient (r) of 0.997 for 2-mers; point-wise regression at 6-mer resolution yields R 2 = 0.859, highlighting accurate recapitulation of key motifs (e.g., TATAAT). ### 3.2. Generating stationary-phase promoters using DiPro
To design novel promoters with desired functions, we employed a masking strategy by providing a partially masked sequence for the model to generate the missing area. First, stationary-phase promoters were collected and analyzed according to their strength. Stationary-phase promoters regulated by σ38, also known as RpoS [ 32 ], exhibit pronounced AT-rich extended −10 features [ 33 ], weaker −35 dependence, and −35/−10 spacing concentrated at 16–18 bp, with distinctive composition between −10 and the TSS. σ38-annotated samples were included during training, and stationary-phase–targeted sequences were generated by inpainting: for each high-expression σ38 seed, multiple non-overlapping 6-mer windows were masked and completed by the diffusion model, preserving global spacing while reshaping local content. This strategy yielded 5000 candidates. Each candidate was encoded as an 87-dimensional feature vector and the dimensionality was reduced to 10 via PCA. Bayesian clustering using a full-covariance GMM was then applied in this reduced space. The number of clusters was objectively determined by scanning K from 2 to 10 and selecting the value that minimized the BIC, which identified K = 3 as the optimal model ( Fig. S3 ). The resulting GMM partitioned the candidates into three compositionally distinct groups with calibrated posterior probabilities ( Fig. 3 A).
Conditional generation and clustering of stationary-phase (σ 38 -regulated) promoters.

### 3.3. Characterizing the activity of generated stationary phase promoters
The transcriptional activity of the generated stationary-phase promoters was evaluated using GFP as a reporter [ 34 ]. Fluorescence intensity was monitored at key time points (10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 45, 50, 55 and 60 h, consistent with Fig. 5 ) throughout a 60 h fermentation period to fully capture the temporal transcriptional activity and stationary-phase-specific activation pattern ( Fig. 4 ). To ensure representativeness and structural diversity for reliable experimental validation, 60 promoter candidates were strictly selected from 5000 generated sequences based on four quantitative criteria: (1) balanced sampling across clusters with 20 candidates selected from each of Cluster 0, Cluster 1, and Cluster 2; (2) high-confidence filtering with a GMM posterior classification probability of no less than 0.7; (3) preference for candidates harboring conserved −35/−10 core motifs and canonical 16–18 bp spacer length; (4) removal of sequences with over 90% identity to eliminate redundant sequences and maximize structural diversity. Promoter sequences were randomly selected from each computationally defined cluster for experimental validation ( Table S1 ). To more specifically and rigorously evaluate the stationary-phase activity of synthetic promoters, two well-characterized σ 38 -regulated native stationary-phase promoters, P katE and P bola , were included as stationary-phase positive controls, in addition to the strong constitutive promoter J23119 (as a general strength benchmark). Our results demonstrated that 49 out of the 60 tested promoters (81.6%) exhibited significantly higher activity than the negative control. However, all synthetic promoters showed lower strength than the strong constitutive promoter J23119 ( Fig. 4 ), which is one of the most active constitutive promoters [ 35 ] and was used as a general positive control for promoter strength. Among the generated promoters, the most active one, P11, reached 79.6% of the total activity of J23119, and more import

### 3.4. Characterizing time-dependent activity of the generated stationary-phase promoters
Next, we characterized the time-dependent activity of the generated promoters by tracking the OD 600 and fluorescent intensity of the top 20 most active designs. To eliminate ambiguity and enable quantitative classification, we strictly defined four growth phases based on fermentation time: (1) Exponential growth phase: 0–20 h (rapid OD 600 increase, negligible stationary-phase promoter activity); (2) Early stationary phase: 20–30 h (OD 600 stabilization, initial promoter activation); (3) Middle stationary phase: 30–50 h (peak promoter activity); (4) Late stationary phase: 50–60 h (sustained activity under nutrient limitation). Promoters were categorized by the first time point of significant fluorescence elevation relative to the exponential phase. The time-dependent activation profiles of the native stationary-phase promoters P katE and P bola were also monitored as references, and both exhibited typical mid-stationary-phase activation characteristics, which were consistent with the main activation trend of our synthetic promoters. We found that 14 promoters were active before the 20 h time point, when OD 600 stabilized, indicating they are not strictly stationary-phase promoters ( Fig. 5 ). Furthermore, even among stationary-phase promoters, we observed variation in their timing of activation, likely due to sensing different cellular stresses. Based on the above quantitative time criteria, we divided the stationary phase into three periods: early, middle, and late. We found that 20% and 60% of these promoters were activated in the early and middle phases, respectively, and displayed higher overall induction activity than those activated late. This may be attributed to the relatively abundant nutrient availability during the early to middle stationary phase, whereas promoters induced later are likely constrained by nutrient depletion and deteriorating environmental conditions.

### 3.5. Induction of cell lysis using stationary phase promoters, a case study
As a proof-of-concept for the functional application of our designed promoters, we implemented a programmed cell lysis system using stationary-phase-specific promoters to control the expression of a lethal protein. To rigorously validate lysis efficiency, the negative control without the CoIM cassette and the strong constitutive promoter J23119 (added in Fig. 6 B) were included as controls. We selected three of the strongest generated promoters, each demonstrating activation during the early (P05), middle (P14), and late (P11) stationary phase, respectively. These promoters were used to drive the expression of the cell lysis protein CoIM ( Fig. 6 A), which was chosen for its previously reported high efficacy in degrading E. coli cell walls even under high-density cultivation conditions [ 36 ]. The performance of this system was evaluated by monitoring the growth of engineered strains over a 60 h fermentation period. As shown in Fig. 6 B, the negative control strain, which lacked the CoIM expression cassette, exhibited robust growth, reaching a final OD 600 of approximately 8. The constitutive promoter J23119 mediated complete cell lysis and served as the positive control for maximal lysis activity. In stark contrast, strains carrying the CoIM gene under the control of the synthetic promoters showed markedly impaired growth, confirming the functional triggering of cell lysis.
Schematic of the cell lysis experiment.

### 4. Discussion
This study developed a stable diffusion-based model, DiPro, for the de novo generation of promoters. Initial analyses demonstrated that the designed promoters accurately recapitulated key features of the natural training set, as evidenced by sequence logos, k-mer spectra, and functional motif distributions [ 37 ]. We then employed DiPro to design stationary-phase promoters by inpainting randomly masked regions within seed sequences. Subsequently, we developed a Bayesian-based machine learning model to cluster the generated promoters. Representative samples from each cluster were experimentally characterized, revealing that 81.6% exhibited induction activity. Furthermore, we found that these stationary-phase promoters were activated during three distinct stages (early, middle, and late). Leveraging this temporal precision, we used selected promoters to drive expression of the cell lysis protein CoIM, thereby regulating cell death. Notably, promoter P05 triggered cell lysis with high efficiency. This work establishes a novel methodological framework and validates its practical utility.
Generative networks are now well-established for promoter design. Pioneering GAN-based models demonstrated the feasibility of designing functional E. coli promoters [ 15 ], and when combined with a predictive network, enabled the design of promoters with tunable activity levels. Subsequently, GAN-based frameworks were adapted for designing eukaryotic promoters [ 16 ], enabling applications in Saccharomyces cerevisiae with potential extension to filamentous fungi and microalgae [ 38 ]. In more recent work, diffusion models have been applied. However, early implementations relied on a separate promoter recognition model to guide generation [ 39 ]. This limitation has been addressed by later approaches. Unconditional de novo generation and functional validation of synthetic promoters with a diffusion model

### Abstract
Generative neural networks enable de novo design of synthetic genetic elements. Here, we present DiPro, an unconditional diffusion model that learns E. coli promoter features to generate novel sequences without conditional input. DiPro directly generates 50-bp promoter sequences from Gaussian noise using a time-conditioned Transformer denoiser, without auxiliary discriminators or recognizers. DiPro accurately recapitulates natural promoter statistics, including sequence motifs, k-mer spectra, conserved −35/−10 spacing (16–18 bp). Over 90% of generated sequences were classified as real promoters by an independent recognizer, indicating high structural fidelity. To design stationary-phase–specific promoters, generation was guided by inpainting randomly masked regions (three non-overlapping 6-mers, 18 bp) within sigma38-associated (σ 38 ) seed sequences, yielding 5000 candidates while preserving global promoter architecture. Bayesian classification resolved these sequences into three distinct clusters with divergent −35/−10 composition and motif conservation. Experimentally, 81.6% of tested promoters exhibited stationary-phase activity, with the strongest variant reaching 79.6% of the activity of the constitutive promoter J23119. Promoters displayed distinct activation timing, reflecting heterogeneous stress responses. As a proof-of-concept, selected promoters were used to drive a lysis protein, achieving phase-specific and tunable cell lysis that matched promoter activation timing, with early-phase promoters reducing culture density to an optical density at 600 nm of approximately 1.5–2.0. Together, these results establish DiPro as a generative framework for creating functional bacterial promoters with programmable temporal dynamics, offering a new tool for synthetic biology and metabolic engineering.

### 1. Introduction
Promoters are essential cis -regulatory DNA sequences that control the transcription rate of downstream genes and thereby determine protein expression levels in living cells [ 1 ]. The activity of promoters directly influences both protein abundance and secretion efficiency, making them critical targets for optimizing recombinant protein production and metabolic flux in microorganisms [ 2 , 3 ]. Despite extensive efforts to engineer strong constitutive promoters, it remains challenging to design promoters with activities surpassing those of the strongest natural counterparts or time-dependent samples that regulates cell behavior at specific period [ 4 , 5 ]. In Escherichia coli , growth-phase–dependent promoters exhibit dynamic transcriptional activity that varies across exponential and stationary phases, enabling precise temporal regulation of gene expression [ 6 , 7 ]. These promoters are controlled by cellular physiological states and global regulators such as σ 70 , ensuring coordinated responses to environmental and metabolic changes [ 8 ]. Understanding and engineering such phase-specific promoters is crucial for optimizing dynamic gene expression in synthetic and metabolic circuits [ 9 ]. Their rational design can improve time-dependent protein production, stress adaptation, and lifespan control in engineered microbial systems [ 10 ].
Bioinformatics tools have long been used to dissect promoter sequence–function relationships and to guide de novo design by identifying conserved features such as the −35 and −10 motifs and their optimal spacing [ 11 ]. These motif-centric and statistical approaches together with synthetic-library screens have clarified key determinants of promoter strength, for example, the TTTACG/−35 and TATAAT/−10 combination and an ∼17-bp spacer [ 12 ], but they struggle to capture the higher-order, nonlinear interactions among sequence elements that ultimately govern activity, leaving accurate strength prediction challenging [ 13 ]. ### 2.5. Model architecture
DiPro is a diffusion language model (DLM) built on a Transformer [ 28 ] backbone comprising an embedding layer, a time-conditioned encoder, and a diffusion module, as shown in Fig. 1 . Tokens are embedded in a 512-dimensional space and normalized with LayerNorm. The encoder stacks 12 layers with 8-head self-attention and GELU feed-forward blocks at fourfold width, using rotary position embeddings (RoPE) for positional encoding. Diffusion time is injected via adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN): a learned sinusoidal time embedding produces per-layer scale (γ) and shift (β) that modulate normalized activations:
Schematic of the DiPro model architecture and workflow.
The model takes Gaussian noise (z ∼ N(0,I)) and time step (t) as inputs, with token embedding (10 tokens, 512 dimensions) and learned sinusoidal time embedding (128 dimensions) fed into a time-conditioned Transformer denoiser. The denoiser comprises multi-head attention (8 heads, RoPE-32), AdaLayerNorm (AdaLN), and feed-forward networks (FFN, 512→2048→512); reverse diffusion iteratively refines the noisy input to generate 50-bp promoter sequences. Training losses include diffusion loss (MSE) and reconstruction loss (CE); the output projection layer and LM Head produce logits, with ArgMax used to decode final DNA sequences. ### 2.6. Diffusion process
We use a continuous-time diffusion framework [ 29 ] with t ∈ [0, 1] . In training, forward diffusion adds Gaussian noise to the clean embedding X 0 :
X t = √(γ(t)) X 0 + √(1-γ(t)) ε, ε ∼ N(0, I),
cos 2 (( (t + 0.0002))/(2 (1.00025))) . Time steps t are sampled uniformly from U(0.001, 0.999) to avoid degenerate extremes. During inference, reverse diffusion starts from pure Gaussian noise z and iteratively denoises with the trained Transformer estimator, updating at each step as
X t -Δ t = √(γ(t-Δ t)) f θ (X t , t) + √(1-γ(t-Δ t)) ε'.

### 2.8. Evaluation of generated sequence quality
We conducted a multi-level quantitative comparison between generated promoters and the training set to assess sequence quality and functional fidelity. First, we used information-theoretic sequence logos derived from per-position base frequencies and Shannon entropy, with I = 2 - H and H = -∑ p i
p i , to visualize conservation at key regulatory elements such as the −35 and −10 boxes. This approach quantifies positional specificity and provides direct evidence for the preservation of core regulatory motifs.

### 3.1. Establishing DiPro to unconditional generate de novo promoters
We introduce DiPro, an unconditional diffusion framework for de novo generation of non-natural promoters. The model starts from Gaussian noise and, through a time-conditioned Transformer denoiser, iteratively generates 50-bp promoter sequences without relying on an auxiliary discriminator or a separate recognizer ( Fig. 1 ). DiPro was benchmarked against three representative deep generative models for promoter design, including generative adversarial networks, variational autoencoders, and early diffusion-based generative tools. The performance was assessed by comparing conserved motifs, spatial distributions of key motifs, and the −35 to −10 spacing statistics ( Fig. 2 A). To select the training epochs with the best performance, we visualized the sequence-logo comparisons of sequences generated during training and predicted the real promoter portion (RPP, defined as the fraction of generated sequences classified as authentic promoters by PromoR) in the generated data using PromoR [ 31 ], a tool previously shown to achieve high accuracy in classifying real and artificial promoters ( Fig. 1 C and D).
Unconditional de novo generation of Escherichia coli promoters by DiPro recapitulates natural promoter features.
(A) Sequence logos of natural promoters and DiPro-generated promoters (post-training) aligned to the transcription start site (TSS). Both sets exhibit conserved −35 and −10 regions, with the classical TT motif at −35 and TATAAT motif at −10 showing consistent positional alignment. (B) Real Promoter Portion (RPP) of generated sequences (assessed by PromoR) across training epochs, reaching &gt;90% stability after 600 epochs. (C) K-mer spectrum correlation between natural and DiPro-generated promoters. 2-mer to 6-mer distributions show high agreement, with a Pearson correlation coefficient (r) of 0.997 for 2-mers; point-wise regression at 6-mer resolution yields R 2 = 0.859, highlighting accurate recapitulation of key motifs (e.g., TATAAT). ### 3.2. Generating stationary-phase promoters using DiPro
To design novel promoters with desired functions, we employed a masking strategy by providing a partially masked sequence for the model to generate the missing area. First, stationary-phase promoters were collected and analyzed according to their strength. Stationary-phase promoters regulated by σ38, also known as RpoS [ 32 ], exhibit pronounced AT-rich extended −10 features [ 33 ], weaker −35 dependence, and −35/−10 spacing concentrated at 16–18 bp, with distinctive composition between −10 and the TSS. σ38-annotated samples were included during training, and stationary-phase–targeted sequences were generated by inpainting: for each high-expression σ38 seed, multiple non-overlapping 6-mer windows were masked and completed by the diffusion model, preserving global spacing while reshaping local content. This strategy yielded 5000 candidates. Each candidate was encoded as an 87-dimensional feature vector and the dimensionality was reduced to 10 via PCA. Bayesian clustering using a full-covariance GMM was then applied in this reduced space. The number of clusters was objectively determined by scanning K from 2 to 10 and selecting the value that minimized the BIC, which identified K = 3 as the optimal model ( Fig. S3 ). The resulting GMM partitioned the candidates into three compositionally distinct groups with calibrated posterior probabilities ( Fig. 3 A).
Conditional generation and clustering of stationary-phase (σ 38 -regulated) promoters.

### 3.3. Characterizing the activity of generated stationary phase promoters
The transcriptional activity of the generated stationary-phase promoters was evaluated using GFP as a reporter [ 34 ]. Fluorescence intensity was monitored at key time points (10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 45, 50, 55 and 60 h, consistent with Fig. 5 ) throughout a 60 h fermentation period to fully capture the temporal transcriptional activity and stationary-phase-specific activation pattern ( Fig. 4 ). To ensure representativeness and structural diversity for reliable experimental validation, 60 promoter candidates were strictly selected from 5000 generated sequences based on four quantitative criteria: (1) balanced sampling across clusters with 20 candidates selected from each of Cluster 0, Cluster 1, and Cluster 2; (2) high-confidence filtering with a GMM posterior classification probability of no less than 0.7; (3) preference for candidates harboring conserved −35/−10 core motifs and canonical 16–18 bp spacer length; (4) removal of sequences with over 90% identity to eliminate redundant sequences and maximize structural diversity. Promoter sequences were randomly selected from each computationally defined cluster for experimental validation ( Table S1 ). To more specifically and rigorously evaluate the stationary-phase activity of synthetic promoters, two well-characterized σ 38 -regulated native stationary-phase promoters, P katE and P bola , were included as stationary-phase positive controls, in addition to the strong constitutive promoter J23119 (as a general strength benchmark). Our results demonstrated that 49 out of the 60 tested promoters (81.6%) exhibited significantly higher activity than the negative control. However, all synthetic promoters showed lower strength than the strong constitutive promoter J23119 ( Fig. 4 ), which is one of the most active constitutive promoters [ 35 ] and was used as a general positive control for promoter strength. Among the generated promoters, the most active one, P11, reached 79.6% of the total activity of J23119, and more import

### 3.4. Characterizing time-dependent activity of the generated stationary-phase promoters
Next, we characterized the time-dependent activity of the generated promoters by tracking the OD 600 and fluorescent intensity of the top 20 most active designs. To eliminate ambiguity and enable quantitative classification, we strictly defined four growth phases based on fermentation time: (1) Exponential growth phase: 0–20 h (rapid OD 600 increase, negligible stationary-phase promoter activity); (2) Early stationary phase: 20–30 h (OD 600 stabilization, initial promoter activation); (3) Middle stationary phase: 30–50 h (peak promoter activity); (4) Late stationary phase: 50–60 h (sustained activity under nutrient limitation). Promoters were categorized by the first time point of significant fluorescence elevation relative to the exponential phase. The time-dependent activation profiles of the native stationary-phase promoters P katE and P bola were also monitored as references, and both exhibited typical mid-stationary-phase activation characteristics, which were consistent with the main activation trend of our synthetic promoters. We found that 14 promoters were active before the 20 h time point, when OD 600 stabilized, indicating they are not strictly stationary-phase promoters ( Fig. 5 ). Furthermore, even among stationary-phase promoters, we observed variation in their timing of activation, likely due to sensing different cellular stresses. Based on the above quantitative time criteria, we divided the stationary phase into three periods: early, middle, and late. We found that 20% and 60% of these promoters were activated in the early and middle phases, respectively, and displayed higher overall induction activity than those activated late. This may be attributed to the relatively abundant nutrient availability during the early to middle stationary phase, whereas promoters induced later are likely constrained by nutrient depletion and deteriorating environmental conditions.

### 3.5. Induction of cell lysis using stationary phase promoters, a case study
As a proof-of-concept for the functional application of our designed promoters, we implemented a programmed cell lysis system using stationary-phase-specific promoters to control the expression of a lethal protein. To rigorously validate lysis efficiency, the negative control without the CoIM cassette and the strong constitutive promoter J23119 (added in Fig. 6 B) were included as controls. We selected three of the strongest generated promoters, each demonstrating activation during the early (P05), middle (P14), and late (P11) stationary phase, respectively. These promoters were used to drive the expression of the cell lysis protein CoIM ( Fig. 6 A), which was chosen for its previously reported high efficacy in degrading E. coli cell walls even under high-density cultivation conditions [ 36 ]. The performance of this system was evaluated by monitoring the growth of engineered strains over a 60 h fermentation period. As shown in Fig. 6 B, the negative control strain, which lacked the CoIM expression cassette, exhibited robust growth, reaching a final OD 600 of approximately 8. The constitutive promoter J23119 mediated complete cell lysis and served as the positive control for maximal lysis activity. In stark contrast, strains carrying the CoIM gene under the control of the synthetic promoters showed markedly impaired growth, confirming the functional triggering of cell lysis.
Schematic of the cell lysis experiment.

### 4. Discussion
This study developed a stable diffusion-based model, DiPro, for the de novo generation of promoters. Initial analyses demonstrated that the designed promoters accurately recapitulated key features of the natural training set, as evidenced by sequence logos, k-mer spectra, and functional motif distributions [ 37 ]. We then employed DiPro to design stationary-phase promoters by inpainting randomly masked regions within seed sequences. Subsequently, we developed a Bayesian-based machine learning model to cluster the generated promoters. Representative samples from each cluster were experimentally characterized, revealing that 81.6% exhibited induction activity. Furthermore, we found that these stationary-phase promoters were activated during three distinct stages (early, middle, and late). Leveraging this temporal precision, we used selected promoters to drive expression of the cell lysis protein CoIM, thereby regulating cell death. Notably, promoter P05 triggered cell lysis with high efficiency. This work establishes a novel methodological framework and validates its practical utility.
Generative networks are now well-established for promoter design. Pioneering GAN-based models demonstrated the feasibility of designing functional E. coli promoters [ 15 ], and when combined with a predictive network, enabled the design of promoters with tunable activity levels. Subsequently, GAN-based frameworks were adapted for designing eukaryotic promoters [ 16 ], enabling applications in Saccharomyces cerevisiae with potential extension to filamentous fungi and microalgae [ 38 ]. In more recent work, diffusion models have been applied. However, early implementations relied on a separate promoter recognition model to guide generation [ 39 ]. This limitation has been addressed by later approaches. Unconditional de novo generation and functional validation of synthetic promoters with a diffusion model

### Abstract
Generative neural networks enable de novo design of synthetic genetic elements. Here, we present DiPro, an unconditional diffusion model that learns E. coli promoter features to generate novel sequences without conditional input. DiPro directly generates 50-bp promoter sequences from Gaussian noise using a time-conditioned Transformer denoiser, without auxiliary discriminators or recognizers. DiPro accurately recapitulates natural promoter statistics, including sequence motifs, k-mer spectra, conserved −35/−10 spacing (16–18 bp). Over 90% of generated sequences were classified as real promoters by an independent recognizer, indicating high structural fidelity. To design stationary-phase–specific promoters, generation was guided by inpainting randomly masked regions (three non-overlapping 6-mers, 18 bp) within sigma38-associated (σ 38 ) seed sequences, yielding 5000 candidates while preserving global promoter architecture. Bayesian classification resolved these sequences into three distinct clusters with divergent −35/−10 composition and motif conservation. Experimentally, 81.6% of tested promoters exhibited stationary-phase activity, with the strongest variant reaching 79.6% of the activity of the constitutive promoter J23119. Promoters displayed distinct activation timing, reflecting heterogeneous stress responses. As a proof-of-concept, selected promoters were used to drive a lysis protein, achieving phase-specific and tunable cell lysis that matched promoter activation timing, with early-phase promoters reducing culture density to an optical density at 600 nm of approximately 1.5–2.0. Together, these results establish DiPro as a generative framework for creating functional bacterial promoters with programmable temporal dynamics, offering a new tool for synthetic biology and metabolic engineering.

### 1. Introduction
Promoters are essential cis -regulatory DNA sequences that control the transcription rate of downstream genes and thereby determine protein expression levels in living cells [ 1 ]. The activity of promoters directly influences both protein abundance and secretion efficiency, making them critical targets for optimizing recombinant protein production and metabolic flux in microorganisms [ 2 , 3 ]. Despite extensive efforts to engineer strong constitutive promoters, it remains challenging to design promoters with activities surpassing those of the strongest natural counterparts or time-dependent samples that regulates cell behavior at specific period [ 4 , 5 ]. In Escherichia coli , growth-phase–dependent promoters exhibit dynamic transcriptional activity that varies across exponential and stationary phases, enabling precise temporal regulation of gene expression [ 6 , 7 ]. These promoters are controlled by cellular physiological states and global regulators such as σ 70 , ensuring coordinated responses to environmental and metabolic changes [ 8 ]. Understanding and engineering such phase-specific promoters is crucial for optimizing dynamic gene expression in synthetic and metabolic circuits [ 9 ]. Their rational design can improve time-dependent protein production, stress adaptation, and lifespan control in engineered microbial systems [ 10 ].
Bioinformatics tools have long been used to dissect promoter sequence–function relationships and to guide de novo design by identifying conserved features such as the −35 and −10 motifs and their optimal spacing [ 11 ]. These motif-centric and statistical approaches together with synthetic-library screens have clarified key determinants of promoter strength, for example, the TTTACG/−35 and TATAAT/−10 combination and an ∼17-bp spacer [ 12 ], but they struggle to capture the higher-order, nonlinear interactions among sequence elements that ultimately govern activity, leaving accurate strength prediction challenging [ 13 ]. ### 2.5. Model architecture
DiPro is a diffusion language model (DLM) built on a Transformer [ 28 ] backbone comprising an embedding layer, a time-conditioned encoder, and a diffusion module, as shown in Fig. 1 . Tokens are embedded in a 512-dimensional space and normalized with LayerNorm. The encoder stacks 12 layers with 8-head self-attention and GELU feed-forward blocks at fourfold width, using rotary position embeddings (RoPE) for positional encoding. Diffusion time is injected via adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN): a learned sinusoidal time embedding produces per-layer scale (γ) and shift (β) that modulate normalized activations:
Schematic of the DiPro model architecture and workflow.
The model takes Gaussian noise (z ∼ N(0,I)) and time step (t) as inputs, with token embedding (10 tokens, 512 dimensions) and learned sinusoidal time embedding (128 dimensions) fed into a time-conditioned Transformer denoiser. The denoiser comprises multi-head attention (8 heads, RoPE-32), AdaLayerNorm (AdaLN), and feed-forward networks (FFN, 512→2048→512); reverse diffusion iteratively refines the noisy input to generate 50-bp promoter sequences. Training losses include diffusion loss (MSE) and reconstruction loss (CE); the output projection layer and LM Head produce logits, with ArgMax used to decode final DNA sequences. ### 2.6. Diffusion process
We use a continuous-time diffusion framework [ 29 ] with t ∈ [0, 1] . In training, forward diffusion adds Gaussian noise to the clean embedding X 0 :
X t = √(γ(t)) X 0 + √(1-γ(t)) ε, ε ∼ N(0, I),
cos 2 (( (t + 0.0002))/(2 (1.00025))) . Time steps t are sampled uniformly from U(0.001, 0.999) to avoid degenerate extremes. During inference, reverse diffusion starts from pure Gaussian noise z and iteratively denoises with the trained Transformer estimator, updating at each step as
X t -Δ t = √(γ(t-Δ t)) f θ (X t , t) + √(1-γ(t-Δ t)) ε'.

### 2.8. Evaluation of generated sequence quality
We conducted a multi-level quantitative comparison between generated promoters and the training set to assess sequence quality and functional fidelity. First, we used information-theoretic sequence logos derived from per-position base frequencies and Shannon entropy, with I = 2 - H and H = -∑ p i
p i , to visualize conservation at key regulatory elements such as the −35 and −10 boxes. This approach quantifies positional specificity and provides direct evidence for the preservation of core regulatory motifs.

### 3.1. Establishing DiPro to unconditional generate de novo promoters
We introduce DiPro, an unconditional diffusion framework for de novo generation of non-natural promoters. The model starts from Gaussian noise and, through a time-conditioned Transformer denoiser, iteratively generates 50-bp promoter sequences without relying on an auxiliary discriminator or a separate recognizer ( Fig. 1 ). DiPro was benchmarked against three representative deep generative models for promoter design, including generative adversarial networks, variational autoencoders, and early diffusion-based generative tools. The performance was assessed by comparing conserved motifs, spatial distributions of key motifs, and the −35 to −10 spacing statistics ( Fig. 2 A). To select the training epochs with the best performance, we visualized the sequence-logo comparisons of sequences generated during training and predicted the real promoter portion (RPP, defined as the fraction of generated sequences classified as authentic promoters by PromoR) in the generated data using PromoR [ 31 ], a tool previously shown to achieve high accuracy in classifying real and artificial promoters ( Fig. 1 C and D).
Unconditional de novo generation of Escherichia coli promoters by DiPro recapitulates natural promoter features.
(A) Sequence logos of natural promoters and DiPro-generated promoters (post-training) aligned to the transcription start site (TSS). Both sets exhibit conserved −35 and −10 regions, with the classical TT motif at −35 and TATAAT motif at −10 showing consistent positional alignment. (B) Real Promoter Portion (RPP) of generated sequences (assessed by PromoR) across training epochs, reaching &gt;90% stability after 600 epochs. (C) K-mer spectrum correlation between natural and DiPro-generated promoters. 2-mer to 6-mer distributions show high agreement, with a Pearson correlation coefficient (r) of 0.997 for 2-mers; point-wise regression at 6-mer resolution yields R 2 = 0.859, highlighting accurate recapitulation of key motifs (e.g., TATAAT). ### 3.2. Generating stationary-phase promoters using DiPro
To design novel promoters with desired functions, we employed a masking strategy by providing a partially masked sequence for the model to generate the missing area. First, stationary-phase promoters were collected and analyzed according to their strength. Stationary-phase promoters regulated by σ38, also known as RpoS [ 32 ], exhibit pronounced AT-rich extended −10 features [ 33 ], weaker −35 dependence, and −35/−10 spacing concentrated at 16–18 bp, with distinctive composition between −10 and the TSS. σ38-annotated samples were included during training, and stationary-phase–targeted sequences were generated by inpainting: for each high-expression σ38 seed, multiple non-overlapping 6-mer windows were masked and completed by the diffusion model, preserving global spacing while reshaping local content. This strategy yielded 5000 candidates. Each candidate was encoded as an 87-dimensional feature vector and the dimensionality was reduced to 10 via PCA. Bayesian clustering using a full-covariance GMM was then applied in this reduced space. The number of clusters was objectively determined by scanning K from 2 to 10 and selecting the value that minimized the BIC, which identified K = 3 as the optimal model ( Fig. S3 ). The resulting GMM partitioned the candidates into three compositionally distinct groups with calibrated posterior probabilities ( Fig. 3 A).
Conditional generation and clustering of stationary-phase (σ 38 -regulated) promoters.

### 3.3. Characterizing the activity of generated stationary phase promoters
The transcriptional activity of the generated stationary-phase promoters was evaluated using GFP as a reporter [ 34 ]. Fluorescence intensity was monitored at key time points (10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 45, 50, 55 and 60 h, consistent with Fig. 5 ) throughout a 60 h fermentation period to fully capture the temporal transcriptional activity and stationary-phase-specific activation pattern ( Fig. 4 ). To ensure representativeness and structural diversity for reliable experimental validation, 60 promoter candidates were strictly selected from 5000 generated sequences based on four quantitative criteria: (1) balanced sampling across clusters with 20 candidates selected from each of Cluster 0, Cluster 1, and Cluster 2; (2) high-confidence filtering with a GMM posterior classification probability of no less than 0.7; (3) preference for candidates harboring conserved −35/−10 core motifs and canonical 16–18 bp spacer length; (4) removal of sequences with over 90% identity to eliminate redundant sequences and maximize structural diversity. Promoter sequences were randomly selected from each computationally defined cluster for experimental validation ( Table S1 ). To more specifically and rigorously evaluate the stationary-phase activity of synthetic promoters, two well-characterized σ 38 -regulated native stationary-phase promoters, P katE and P bola , were included as stationary-phase positive controls, in addition to the strong constitutive promoter J23119 (as a general strength benchmark). Our results demonstrated that 49 out of the 60 tested promoters (81.6%) exhibited significantly higher activity than the negative control. However, all synthetic promoters showed lower strength than the strong constitutive promoter J23119 ( Fig. 4 ), which is one of the most active constitutive promoters [ 35 ] and was used as a general positive control for promoter strength. Among the generated promoters, the most active one, P11, reached 79.6% of the total activity of J23119, and more import

### 3.4. Characterizing time-dependent activity of the generated stationary-phase promoters
Next, we characterized the time-dependent activity of the generated promoters by tracking the OD 600 and fluorescent intensity of the top 20 most active designs. To eliminate ambiguity and enable quantitative classification, we strictly defined four growth phases based on fermentation time: (1) Exponential growth phase: 0–20 h (rapid OD 600 increase, negligible stationary-phase promoter activity); (2) Early stationary phase: 20–30 h (OD 600 stabilization, initial promoter activation); (3) Middle stationary phase: 30–50 h (peak promoter activity); (4) Late stationary phase: 50–60 h (sustained activity under nutrient limitation). Promoters were categorized by the first time point of significant fluorescence elevation relative to the exponential phase. The time-dependent activation profiles of the native stationary-phase promoters P katE and P bola were also monitored as references, and both exhibited typical mid-stationary-phase activation characteristics, which were consistent with the main activation trend of our synthetic promoters. We found that 14 promoters were active before the 20 h time point, when OD 600 stabilized, indicating they are not strictly stationary-phase promoters ( Fig. 5 ). Furthermore, even among stationary-phase promoters, we observed variation in their timing of activation, likely due to sensing different cellular stresses. Based on the above quantitative time criteria, we divided the stationary phase into three periods: early, middle, and late. We found that 20% and 60% of these promoters were activated in the early and middle phases, respectively, and displayed higher overall induction activity than those activated late. This may be attributed to the relatively abundant nutrient availability during the early to middle stationary phase, whereas promoters induced later are likely constrained by nutrient depletion and deteriorating environmental conditions.

### 3.5. Induction of cell lysis using stationary phase promoters, a case study
As a proof-of-concept for the functional application of our designed promoters, we implemented a programmed cell lysis system using stationary-phase-specific promoters to control the expression of a lethal protein. To rigorously validate lysis efficiency, the negative control without the CoIM cassette and the strong constitutive promoter J23119 (added in Fig. 6 B) were included as controls. We selected three of the strongest generated promoters, each demonstrating activation during the early (P05), middle (P14), and late (P11) stationary phase, respectively. These promoters were used to drive the expression of the cell lysis protein CoIM ( Fig. 6 A), which was chosen for its previously reported high efficacy in degrading E. coli cell walls even under high-density cultivation conditions [ 36 ]. The performance of this system was evaluated by monitoring the growth of engineered strains over a 60 h fermentation period. As shown in Fig. 6 B, the negative control strain, which lacked the CoIM expression cassette, exhibited robust growth, reaching a final OD 600 of approximately 8. The constitutive promoter J23119 mediated complete cell lysis and served as the positive control for maximal lysis activity. In stark contrast, strains carrying the CoIM gene under the control of the synthetic promoters showed markedly impaired growth, confirming the functional triggering of cell lysis.
Schematic of the cell lysis experiment.

### 4. Discussion
This study developed a stable diffusion-based model, DiPro, for the de novo generation of promoters. Initial analyses demonstrated that the designed promoters accurately recapitulated key features of the natural training set, as evidenced by sequence logos, k-mer spectra, and functional motif distributions [ 37 ]. We then employed DiPro to design stationary-phase promoters by inpainting randomly masked regions within seed sequences. Subsequently, we developed a Bayesian-based machine learning model to cluster the generated promoters. Representative samples from each cluster were experimentally characterized, revealing that 81.6% exhibited induction activity. Furthermore, we found that these stationary-phase promoters were activated during three distinct stages (early, middle, and late). Leveraging this temporal precision, we used selected promoters to drive expression of the cell lysis protein CoIM, thereby regulating cell death. Notably, promoter P05 triggered cell lysis with high efficiency. This work establishes a novel methodological framework and validates its practical utility.
Generative networks are now well-established for promoter design. Pioneering GAN-based models demonstrated the feasibility of designing functional E. coli promoters [ 15 ], and when combined with a predictive network, enabled the design of promoters with tunable activity levels. Subsequently, GAN-based frameworks were adapted for designing eukaryotic promoters [ 16 ], enabling applications in Saccharomyces cerevisiae with potential extension to filamentous fungi and microalgae [ 38 ]. In more recent work, diffusion models have been applied. However, early implementations relied on a separate promoter recognition model to guide generation [ 39 ]. This limitation has been addressed by later approaches. Unconditional de novo generation and functional validation of synthetic promoters with a diffusion model
